bodyMarkdown:
If you are researching solar panel installation in Wichita, you may notice that quotes for homes that look similar can come back very different. That is not usually a mystery. A solar quote reflects a set of project variables, from how much electricity you use to what your roof and electrical system need. Understanding those variables helps you read a quote with confidence and ask better questions.

This guide walks through the main factors that shape a solar installation quote and what to ask to see in writing.

## Why no two quotes look the same

Every home is different. Roof shape, shade, electrical equipment, household usage and personal priorities all change what a well-designed system looks like. Two installers can also make different design choices for the same home. A quote is the end result of all those decisions, so the most useful thing you can do is understand the decisions behind it.

## System size and your electricity use

The biggest driver of any design is how much electricity your household uses and how you want the system to serve that use. A full year of utility bills gives the clearest picture, because heating and cooling can change usage a lot from season to season.

Ask each installer how they sized the system and which usage information they used. If you are planning changes, such as an electric vehicle or switching to electric heating, mention them. They can change the size of system that makes sense for your home.

## Roof and site conditions

Your roof shapes both the design and the work involved. The U.S. Department of Energy's [Homeowner's Guide to Going Solar](https://www.energy.gov/eere/solar/homeowners-guide-going-solar) advises: "You should also consider the age of your roof and how long until it will need replacement."

Several site factors can affect a quote:

- The age and condition of the roof, and whether repairs should come first
- How many roof sections the layout uses, and how steep they are
- Shade from trees or nearby buildings
- Whether ground space is being considered instead of the roof

If a quote assumes something about your roof, such as no repairs needed, ask for that assumption in writing.

## Equipment choices

Quotes differ in the equipment they specify. Panels, inverters, mounting hardware and monitoring equipment all vary, and so does how each design arranges them. You do not need to know every component, but you should be able to see what is included and why it was chosen for your home.

Ask each installer to list the main equipment in writing and to explain any choice you do not understand.

## Electrical work and permits

Some homes need electrical work before or during a solar installation, such as changes at the main electrical panel. Permits, inspections and utility paperwork are also part of every project.

The Federal Trade Commission's guide, [Solar Power for Your Home](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/solar-power-your-home), says "Bids should have specific details in writing about the system, including" its size, the full installation work and any building or electrical permit fees. That is a good standard to hold every quote to. If electrical upgrades or permit work are expected, they should be visible in the written quote rather than discovered later.

## Battery backup

Adding battery backup changes the design and the quote. The questions shift to which circuits you want running during an outage, where the equipment would go and how it works with the panels.

If backup power matters to you, ask for quotes with and without a battery so you can see how the choice changes the project. Our page on [battery backup and storage](https://www.logic-solar.com/services/battery) covers the questions to ask about essential circuits.

## Your own priorities

Your preferences shape a quote too. Some homeowners care most about how the array looks from the street and prefer to leave a front-facing roof section empty. Others want to keep room for future expansion or want ground space considered instead of the roof. Tell each installer what matters to you, so the quotes reflect your priorities rather than assumptions.

## What to ask to see in writing

Before comparing totals, make sure each quote shows:

- The system size and the usage information it was based on
- Which parts of the roof or property are used
- The main equipment included
- Any roof or electrical work the project depends on
- Permits, inspections and utility paperwork, and who handles them
- Whether battery backup is included, and for which circuits

A quote you can follow line by line is one you can actually evaluate.

## A short checklist

- A full year of electricity usage
- Notes on your roof's age and condition
- Planned changes to your home or household
- Your priorities, including whether backup power matters
- A list of what each quote should show in writing
